passage: Teacher's note, Class 5. Akash came to my desk before the trip and asked, “Ma'am, may I go to the shop across the road? I need a pencil, and I'll be back before the bell.” I told him no, because the road is busy and I could not see him from the gate. He nodded, but I could tell he was disappointed. I said, “If you ask me at break, I will send him with the peon.” Akash said, “Okay.” He came back at break, and I sent him with the peon. I think clear reasons help a child accept no. Ms. Aparna.

qa.q: Who was sent with Akash to the shop?
qa.a: The peon.

qa.q: What was Akash probably feeling when he nodded after hearing no?
qa.a: He was probably disappointed but understood, since Ms. Aparna gave a clear reason about the busy road.

qa.q: What did Ms. Aparna do that made a no easier to accept?
qa.a: She gave a reason about safety and offered another way, sending him at break with the peon.

qa.q: How might Akash's request look from Ms. Aparna's side?
qa.a: She could not see him from the gate and worried about the busy road, so her no was about his safety and not about doubting him.

grounding: A child asks may I go and learns that permission depends on safety, timing and trust, and a clear reason helps accept a no.

passage: I watched from the school corridor as Gopika went up to the games teacher. “Sir, can I please stay inside during break? My knee is sore.” The teacher frowned and said, “Show me.” Gopika lifted her trouser hem to show a red patch. The teacher said, “Go to the nurse first and then rest in the library.” Gopika nodded. Arnab, her friend, said, “I thought he'd say no.” “Me too,” said Gopika. I think she was surprised but also relieved. I'm not sure whether the knee hurt as much as she said, but she asked politely and gave a reason.

qa.q: Where did the teacher tell Gopika to go first?
qa.a: To the nurse.

qa.q: What was Gopika probably feeling when the teacher said yes?
qa.a: She was surprised and relieved, since she had expected a no and said “Me too” to Arnab, though the observer is not sure how much the knee hurt.

qa.q: What did Gopika do that helped her request?
qa.a: She asked politely, gave a reason and showed the sore knee when asked.

qa.q: Why might the teacher have asked to see the knee?
qa.a: He may have wanted to check it was real and safe to skip play, which is part of how permission depends on trust.

grounding: A child asks can I please stay inside and permission depends on trust and safety, observed by a bystander.

passage: Saturday: “Mummy, can I cycle to the market alone?” Jomon asked. Rehana shook her head. “Not yet. The main road has trucks, and you've never crossed it on your own. That's the reason, not that I don't trust you.” Jomon kicked the doorstep, but he understood about the trucks. Monday: They cycled the route together after school. Rehana showed him where to get off and walk the bike across, and where to wait. Wednesday: “Can I go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread? It's before the main road.” Rehana thought. “Yes. Straight there, straight back, and ring the bell when you're home.” Jomon was back in twelve minutes, ringing the bell twice.

qa.q: What was Jomon allowed to fetch on Wednesday?
qa.a: He was allowed to go to Joseph Uncle's shop for bread.

qa.q: What was Jomon feeling when he kicked the doorstep?
qa.a: Jomon felt disappointed and frustrated at the no, though he understood the reason about the trucks.

qa.q: Why did Rehana's clear reason help Jomon accept the no?
qa.a: It showed the no was about safety on the main road, not distrust, and led to practice and a smaller yes.

qa.q: What might Rehana have felt when Jomon rang the bell twice?
qa.a: Rehana probably felt relieved and proud that he kept to the plan.

grounding: Shows a child asking permission and learning it depends on safety and trust, with a clear reason helping him accept a no.

passage: Manoj, you're angry I said no to the late film. Sit. Let your Kishore Thatha tell you about the Ther festival when I was eleven. The whole gang was walking across the river to see it at night. I asked my father, “Appa, may I go?” He said no. I shouted that he never trusted me. He waited until I stopped. Then he said, “It's not trust. The river rises fast in this season, and none of you can swim. At night, nobody would see you.” I sulked all evening. Two boys came back soaked and shivering; the water had risen to their chests. The next morning, Appa took me himself, by the bridge.

qa.q: Where was the Ther festival?
qa.a: The Ther festival was across the river.

qa.q: What was young Kishore feeling when his father said no?
qa.a: He felt angry and hurt, believing his father didn't trust him.

qa.q: What choice did his father make that helped Kishore accept the no?
qa.a: He waited for Kishore to finish shouting, gave the real reason about the fast-rising river and the dark, and later took him by the bridge.

qa.q: What was the night like for the two boys who went?
qa.a: They came back soaked and shivering after the river rose to their chests, which showed the danger was real.

grounding: Shows a child asking may I go and learning that permission depends on safety, with a clear reason helping him accept the no.

passage: Alka was already late, keys in one hand, bag slipping off her shoulder, when Lakshmi ran after her down the stairs. “Masi, can I sleep over at Esha's tonight? Please? Everyone's going!” Alka stopped on the landing. There was no time for a long talk. “Not tonight, sweetheart. Here's why: I haven't met Esha's parents yet, and I don't know who else will be there. That's the only reason.” Lakshmi's face crumpled. “But—” “Tonight, ask Esha if her mum can call me. If we talk, next time might be a yes.” Lakshmi nodded, still disappointed. That evening, Esha's mother called. Alka liked her. The next sleepover was a yes.

qa.q: Why did Alka say no to the sleepover?
qa.a: She hadn't met Esha's parents yet and didn't know who else would be there.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi feeling when her face crumpled?
qa.a: Lakshmi felt disappointed and left out, since everyone else was going.

qa.q: How did Alka give a clear reason despite being rushed?
qa.a: She stopped briefly, said exactly why it was a no and gave Lakshmi a step, a phone call, that could lead to a yes next time.

qa.q: What made Alka comfortable saying yes the next time?
qa.a: Talking to Esha's mother on the phone helped Alka trust the plan, so she felt comfortable saying yes.

grounding: Shows a child asking permission and a rushed adult giving a clear reason for the no based on safety and trust.

passage:
"Mummy, may I go to Tanya's party on Saturday? It's at the play zone in the big mall. Everyone's going by auto together."

Parul looked up from her laptop. "What time does it end?"
"Eight… or nine."
"And who's bringing you back?"
Sangeeta shrugged. "We'll share an auto."

Parul shook her head. "Then my answer is no to the auto, and here's why: it'll be dark, I don't know the other parents yet, and four eleven-year-olds alone in an auto at nine isn't safe. But yes to the party if I drop you and pick you up at eight-thirty."

Sangeeta groaned. "So embarrassing." Then she thought. "Can you wait outside the gate, not inside?"
"Deal."

qa.q: Where was Tanya's party?
qa.a: At the play zone in the big mall.

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling when she groaned, "So embarrassing"?
qa.a: Disappointed and a little embarrassed at being dropped and picked up by her mother, though she accepted because she still got to go.

qa.q: Why did Parul's answer make the no easier to accept?
qa.a: She gave clear reasons, the dark, not knowing the parents and safety, and offered a yes to the party with a safer plan.

qa.q: How might Parul feel about making the pickup deal?
qa.a: She probably feels relieved that Sangeeta can go safely and is willing to wait outside the gate to spare her embarrassment.

grounding: It shows a child asking permission and a parent explaining a partial no with clear safety reasons, which helps the child accept it.
